summary: Learners aged 9–10 describe the human life cycle as an ordered, continuous sequence of stages — baby, toddler, child, teenager (adolescence/puberty), adult, elderly — and the characteristic changes at each: rapid early growth and gaining skills (walking, talking) in infancy; the growth spurt and body changes of puberty; maturity in adulthood; and changes of old age (reduced strength, greying hair, slower healing). The organising representation is a life-stage timeline. Puberty is handled factually, sensitively and age-appropriately, framed as a normal, universal stage with wide individual variation in timing. A growth-data strand (plotting height/mass against age; comparing human gestation with other animals) links the topic to working scientifically. The key insight is that development is one unbroken process from birth to old age, not a set of fixed snapshots, and that life stage is defined by developmental changes, not by exact age in years or by body size.
misconceptions: Thinking everyone goes through puberty and other stages at exactly the same age, rather than there being wide individual variation in timing.
Believing growth happens at a constant rate throughout life, missing the fast infancy growth, the pubertal spurt, and the later plateau.
Treating life stages as separate snapshots rather than a continuous developmental process.
Assuming old age is only decline, overlooking that development and change continue across the whole lifespan.
Confusing size/height with life stage (e.g. thinking a tall child is a 'teenager') rather than using developmental changes.

activities.title: Scrub the lifespan timeline and watch change accumulate
steps: Move a slider that runs from birth to old age and watch a single human figure transform in real time: a baby crawls, a toddler takes wobbly first steps, a child, then the teenage growth spurt, a mature adult, and finally an elder with greying hair and a slower gait.
At each position, read a side panel that names the changes happening at the point you have stopped on.
Pause at each stage and say aloud, in your own words, what change is happening and what the body is gaining or losing.
Describe why moving the slider smoothly (rather than jumping between six pictures) shows that 'develop to old age' is one continuous process.
activities.insight: Human development is a continuous process in which change accumulates from birth to old age — not six disconnected snapshots.

activities.title: Draw your own human life-stage timeline
steps: On paper, draw a timeline from birth to old age and mark the stages in order: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult, elderly.
Next to each stage, write one or two characteristic changes (e.g. infancy = fast growth and learning to walk and talk; old age = reduced strength, greying hair, slower healing).
Draw the borders between stages as fuzzy, overlapping bands rather than sharp lines, and explain why.
Check a partner's timeline and discuss any stage where you placed changes differently.
activities.insight: Each life stage is tied to characteristic changes, and the stages form a connected sequence with no abrupt boundaries.

activities.title: Plot height against age and read the growth curve
steps: Plot height (or mass) against age on a chart, using real or realistic growth data from birth to adulthood.

Describe the shape of a height curve in words: rising fast in infancy, still rising but more slowly and steadily in mid-childhood, rising faster again at puberty, then reaching a plateau at adult height (a mass curve may not plateau, because adult mass can keep changing).
Identify the two times in life when humans grow fastest and explain how you found them from the chart.
Compare the amount of height gained in one year during infancy, mid-childhood, and puberty, and say whether growth is the same every year.
activities.insight: Growth does not happen at a constant rate: it comes in spurts (fast in infancy, fast again at puberty) and later plateaus, which connects each stage to a rate of change.

activities.title: Compare gestation periods across animals
steps: Collect or be given gestation (pregnancy) lengths for humans and several other animals.
Order the animals by gestation length and record the data in a simple table.
Describe any pattern you notice (for example, how human gestation compares with that of other animals).
State what question this data helps answer about the very start of the life cycle.
activities.insight: The life cycle starts before birth, and comparing data across animals is a way of investigating development scientifically.

activities.title: Ask a trusted adult persona your growing-up questions
steps: Ask age-appropriate questions about puberty and growing up to a trusted-adult persona (for example, a school-nurse character).
Read factual, sensitive answers framed around the changes of puberty as a normal, universal stage.
Note that people reach puberty at different ages and that this variation is completely normal.
activities.insight: Puberty is a normal, universal stage that happens at different ages for different people, and questions about it can be answered factually.

activities.title: Consolidate: order, match, and reason about two 11-year-olds
steps: Put the life stages in order from baby to elderly.
Match each stage to its characteristic change (e.g. teenager → growth spurt; elderly → slower healing).
Choose what happens at puberty from a set of options, then explain your choice in a sentence.

Reason about a diagnostic case: two children are both exactly 11 years old; one has started a growth spurt and their voice is changing, the other shows none of that yet. Decide whether they are at the same life stage or different ones, and explain what this tells you about how we decide someone's life stage.
activities.insight: Life stage is defined by the developmental changes a person is going through, not by their exact age in years or their body size, so two people the same age can be at different stages, and two people of very different heights can be at the same stage.

checkQuestion: Two children are both exactly 11 years old. One has already started a growth spurt and their voice is changing; the other shows none of that yet. Are they at the same life stage or different ones — and what does your answer tell you about how we decide someone's life stage?
checkAnswer: They can be at different stages: puberty begins at different ages for different people, so two 11-year-olds may be at different points. Life stage is decided by the physical and developmental changes a person is going through, not by their exact age in years.
